title: Rotate Array
corePattern: In-place Array Rotation via Reversal and Cyclic Permutation
interviewTips: Ask if k can be larger than n, negative, or zero, and whether rotation is left or right and must be in-place with O(1) extra space.
Trade-off: extra array is simplest O(n) space, reversal is optimal O(n) time O(1) space and cache-friendly, cyclic replacement is also O(1) space but has more complex index math.
Edge-case tip: always do k %= n first, handle n == 0 or n == 1 early, and verify k == 0 does nothing to avoid invalid reverse ranges.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force with Extra Array
approaches.intuition: Each element at index i moves to (i + k) % n after right rotation. If we can use extra space, just compute destination directly into a new array then copy back.
approaches.theory: Right rotation by k is a permutation p(i) = (i + k) % n. Applying p to all n elements in a separate output array avoids overwrite conflicts. Normalizing k by k %= n handles k >= n. Copy-back makes operation in-place from caller perspective.

timeComplexity.explanation: One pass to place n elements into rotated array plus one pass to copy back, both linear.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Extra array rotated of size n to avoid overwriting during moves.

steps: rotated[(i+3)%7] = nums[i] for all i => rotated = [5,6,7,1,2,3,4]

edgeCases: n == 0: return immediately to avoid modulo by zero
k > n: e.g., n=3 k=4 same as k=1

approaches.name: Approach 2: Three-Step Reversal
approaches.intuition: Reversing the whole array puts the last k elements at front but in reversed order. Reversing the two blocks separately fixes their internal order.
approaches.theory: Let n be length and k %= n. Operation is: reverse[0,n-1], then reverse[0,k-1], then reverse[k,n-1]. Reversal is its own inverse and this composition equals right rotation. Proof by index mapping: after full reverse element at i goes to n-1-i, then block reverses restore correct rotated order. Each element moved twice, total O(n) with O(1) space.

timeComplexity.explanation: Three linear reversals: n + k + (n-k) = 2n operations, so O(n).

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only a few index variables and in-place swaps, no extra array.

edgeCases: k == 0 after modulo: skip to avoid reverse with r = -1
k == n or multiple of n: unchanged
k = n-1: single left shift equivalent

approaches.name: Approach 3: Cyclic Replacements
approaches.intuition: Follow the chain i -> (i+k)%n moving each value forward, holding one displaced value in a temp variable until the cycle closes, then start a new cycle.
approaches.theory: Rotation decomposes into gcd(n,k) disjoint cycles each of length n / gcd(n,k). Starting from each unvisited start, walk the cycle saving prev and writing it to nxt = (cur+k)%n. Count moved elements; when count == n all cycles done. Each element written exactly once.

timeComplexity.explanation: Each of n elements is moved exactly once across all cycles, outer loop runs gcd(n,k) times.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only temp variables prev, cur, nxt, count and start are used.

edgeCases: gcd(n,k) > 1 requires multiple starts, single cycle not enough
k == 0: must early return else infinite loop
